newsitem.title: USA: Lilly says get FTC subpoena on PBMs probe.
newsitem.headline: Lilly says get FTC subpoena on PBMs probe.

text.p: Eli Lilly & Co said Thursday it got a subpoena in October from the U.S. Federal Trade Commission related to its probe of the relationships between drug companies and pharmacy benefits management companies.
"It looks like a continuation of what the FTC started almost two years ago...We are cooperating fully, of course," said Lilly spokesman Edward West.
Shares in Indianapolis-based Lilly closed off 5/8 at 75 on the New York Stock Exchange.

Lilly acquired PCS Health Systems, a company that manages pharmacy benefits plans, in 1994 for $4.1 billion. Shortly earlier, Merck & Co Inc and SmithKline Beecham Plc had also bought pharmacy benefits managers, or PBMs.
The idea behind the acquisitions was they could help steer plan members toward buying drugs made by the parent companies of the PBMs and away from competitors' products.

Merck and SmithKline made their deals before the FTC started asking questions about such acquisitions, but Lilly did not. As a result, Lilly was permitted by the FTC to purchase PCS only under certain conditions.

In its recently filed 10Q quarterly report to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Lilly said the FTC subpoena of last month requested "production of certain documents in connection with a non-public investigation reviewing whether or not the relationships and activities between pharmacy benefit management companies and pharmaceutical companies have violated federal antitrust laws."
Lilly said the FTC's probe included "a review of whether the company has violated the consent decree it entered into at the time it acquired PCS."

When it acquired PCS, Lilly agreed to certain limits on the subsidiary's activities that industry analysts called "firewalls" designed to restrict Lilly's power to reduce free competition among its products and those of rivals.
"The company believes that all of its actions and those of PCS have been lawful, proper and in accordance with the PCS consent decree," Lilly said in its 10Q.
An FTC spokeswoman said the agency could neither confirm nor deny the investigation as reported by Lilly.

"This looks like a continuation of an old saga...Merck and (its PBM unit) Medco have been dealing with the same set of allegations for some time," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell pharmaceuticals analyst Mariola Haggar.
She did not anticipate the FTC probe would hurt Lilly unless it were to escalate into a bigger issue.
The FTC may be checking up on Lilly or possibly considering imposing firewall limits like Lilly's on Merck and SmithKline, as well, speculated Hambrecht & Quist drugs analyst Alex Zisson.
"FTC has been continually revisiting this issue," he said.
